name: Gyeonggi
summary_text: Gyeonggi is scored +0.02 above the national 0.71 on the basis of its role as the origin and continuing custodian of South Korea's student human-rights protections. The model ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province,' was adopted by the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in 2012, and spread to other offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave. When the Seoul Metropolitan Council - controlled by the conservative People Power Party, acting on a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 - abolished Seoul's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing such ordinances (with Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju), and a Gyeonggi teacher was quoted warning that abolishing the ordinance outright 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector.' The deviation is small and the evidence is resident-facing (school non-discrimination rules), carrying limited weight for a traveler per the scoring rules. No Gyeonggi-specific enforcement action, event, incident, or police practice favouring or disfavours a visible trans visitor, and no Gyeonggi council repeal move is on record. (An earlier version of this record credited Gyeonggi's superintendent with blocking Seoul's 2024 repeal; that challenge - the sit-in protest and the July 2024 Supreme Court petition that suspended the abolition - belongs to the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education and its superintendent, not to Gyeonggi. What remains is the origin-and-continued-enforcement record: still the clearest positive sub-national signal in the dossier relative to Seoul (0.66), whose council has twice voted to delete the same ordinance, though its traveler-facing impact remains minimal.)

sources.title: Abolition of student rights ordinance triggers protests - The Korea Times
sources.claim_summary: Korea Times report (28 April 2024) on the Seoul Metropolitan Council's abolition of the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance twelve years after the Seoul office adopted it: the ordinance model was 'first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province'; abolition was pushed by the ruling People Power Party council after an August 2022 campaign by religious groups and parents objecting to its sexual-orientation clause; six regional education offices - Gyeonggi, Gwangju, North Jeolla, South Chungcheong, Incheon and Jeju - still enforced comparable ordinances at publication; the (Seoul) superintendent began a sit-in protest against the abolition, and the opposition-led National Assembly said it would legislate a national student-rights act regardless of regional decisions. A quoted Gyeonggi-based teacher defended the ordinance against wholesale abolition.
